Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 1) The viscera commonly preserved in suspected poisoning includes:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: In suspected poisoning, stomach with contents is commonly preserved. It may contain unabsorbed poison and helps chemical analysis.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 2) The part of intestine commonly preserved in poisoning is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Upper part of small intestine is commonly preserved with viscera. It may contain poison that has passed beyond the stomach.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 3) The length of small intestine commonly preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: About 15–30 cm of upper small intestine is preserved. This is a standard viscera preservation point.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 4) The minimum amount of liver commonly preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Liver is commonly preserved in suspected poisoning. The required amount is about 200–300 g.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 5) The kidney specimen commonly preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Longitudinal half of both kidneys is commonly preserved. This allows detection of poisons excreted through kidneys.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 6) In heavy metal poisoning, the additional specimen preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Heavy metals may accumulate in bone, hair and nails. These specimens are useful in chronic poisoning.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 7) In suspected alcohol poisoning, the preferred specimens include:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option3: Blood, urine, CSF and vitreous humour
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Alcohol analysis is commonly done from blood and urine. CSF and vitreous humour may also be preserved.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 8) In suspected criminal abortion, the additional specimen preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: In suspected criminal abortion, uterus and appendages are preserved. They may show evidence of pregnancy or interference.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 9) In suspected pesticide or insecticide poisoning, the additional specimen preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Pesticides and insecticides may be stored in fat. Fatty tissue is therefore preserved in selected cases.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 10) In suspected strychnine poisoning, the specimen preserved is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: In suspected strychnine poisoning, brain, spinal cord and heart may be preserved. Strychnine acts mainly on the nervous system.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 11) Vomitus is preserved mainly for:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Vomitus may contain poison or drug material. It is therefore useful for chemical analysis.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 12) Stomach washout is a material for:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Stomach washout may contain remnants of poison. It is preserved and sent for chemical analysis.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 13) The usual amount of blood preserved for chemical analysis is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Blood for chemical analysis is usually preserved in about 30 ml amount. The minimum amount mentioned is 10 ml.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 14) The minimum amount of blood for chemical analysis is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: The usual amount is 30 ml, but minimum 10 ml blood may be sent. Blood is important for toxicological estimation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 15) The usual amount of urine preserved for chemical analysis is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Urine is commonly preserved in about 30 ml amount. It is useful because many toxins are excreted in urine.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 16) The most common preservative for viscera is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Saturated solution of common salt is the most common preservative for viscera. It is widely used in toxicological preservation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 17) The preservative used for histopathological examination is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: 10% formol saline is used for histopathology. It preserves tissue architecture for microscopic examination.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 18) The volume of 10% formol saline should usually be:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: For histopathology, 10% formol saline is usually used in 6–10 times the tissue volume. Adequate volume ensures proper fixation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 19) The preservative for blood in toxicology is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option2: Sodium or potassium fluoride with potassium oxalate
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Sodium or potassium fluoride is used with potassium oxalate for blood. Fluoride prevents glycolysis and oxalate acts as anticoagulant.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 20) Potassium oxalate is added to blood mainly as:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Potassium oxalate acts as an anticoagulant in blood samples. It is used along with fluoride in toxicological blood preservation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 21) Sodium fluoride in blood preservation mainly helps to:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Fluoride helps preserve blood by preventing glycolysis and degradation. It is especially important in alcohol estimation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 22) The preservative for urine is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Phenyl mercuric nitrate is used as a preservative for urine. Urine may contain excreted toxins or drugs.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 23) Thymol fluoride is added when suspected poison includes:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Thymol fluoride should be added if alcohol, cyanide or cocaine is suspected. It helps preserve relevant chemical evidence.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 24) Rectified spirit is contraindicated in suspected:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Rectified spirit should not be used in suspected alcohol poisoning. It may interfere with alcohol estimation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 25) Absolute alcohol is used as:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Absolute alcohol is listed among preservatives. Choice of preservative depends on the suspected poison and specimen.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 26) Antemortem clot is characteristically:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Antemortem clot is firmly attached to the vessel wall and has a rough surface. It may show lines of Zahn.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 27) Lines of Zahn are seen in:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Lines of Zahn are characteristic of antemortem clot. They indicate clot formation during life with flowing blood.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 28) Postmortem clot is characteristically:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Postmortem clot is smooth, gelatinous and not firmly attached. It lacks lines of Zahn.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 29) A clot that is not attached to vessel wall is most likely:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Postmortem clots are not attached to the vessel wall. Antemortem clots are attached and rough.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 30) Menstrual blood is characterized by:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option3: Firm clot with lines of Zahn
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Menstrual blood does not clot easily. It contains endometrial cells, vaginal epithelial cells and mucus.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 31) Menstrual blood contains:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option2: Lines of Zahn and fibrin layers only
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option3: Bone marrow cells and hair roots
Specimen Collection, Preservation.option4: Endometrial cells, vaginal epithelial cells and mucus
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Menstrual blood contains endometrial cells, vaginal epithelial cells and mucus. This helps differentiate it from ordinary blood.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 32) Legal digging out of a buried body is called:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Exhumation means legal digging out of a buried body. It is done for identification, autopsy, toxicology or investigation.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 33) Exhumation may be done for:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Exhumation may be done for identification, autopsy, toxicology or investigation of suspicious death. It requires legal authority.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 34) Exhumation is useful in suspected:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Exhumation is performed when investigation is needed after burial. Suspicious death is a common reason.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 35) Chemical preservation of a dead body is called:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Embalming means chemical preservation of the dead body. It delays decomposition.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 36) Embalming is useful for:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Embalming is useful when transport or delayed burial is needed. It chemically preserves the body.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 37) Embalming before toxicology in suspected poisoning is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Embalming before toxicology may interfere with chemical analysis. Therefore, it is dangerous in suspected poisoning.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 38) Autopsy report may be kept pending for:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Autopsy report may be kept pending while awaiting chemical analysis or viscera report. Final opinion may depend on toxicology findings.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 39) Viscera report refers mainly to:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Viscera report means chemical analysis report of preserved viscera. It helps confirm or exclude poisoning.

Specimen Collection, Preservation.question: 40) In suspected alcohol poisoning, the best sample-preservative concept is:
Specimen Collection, Preservation.exp: Blood for alcohol estimation should be preserved with fluoride and potassium oxalate. Rectified spirit should be avoided in suspected alcohol poisoning.
